Classifying Matter: Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space. Matter is either a pure substance or a mixture. A pure substance has a fixed composition and fixed properties. An element is a pure substance made of only one kind of atom, and a compound is two or more elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio, with properties different from those elements. A mixture contains two or more substances that are not chemically combined. A homogeneous mixture (solution) is uniform throughout; a heterogeneous mixture has parts that can be seen. Mixtures can be separated by physical methods such as filtering, distillation, evaporation and magnets.
Physical Properties: A physical property can be observed or measured without changing the substance into a different one. Examples are color, density, melting point, boiling point, hardness, state of matter, solubility, conductivity and malleability. Properties that do not depend on the amount of sample, such as density and melting point, are used to identify a substance. Properties that depend on the amount, such as mass and volume, are used to measure it. Metals are usually shiny, malleable, ductile and good conductors; nonmetals are usually dull, brittle and poor conductors.
Chemical Properties: A chemical property describes how a substance can change into a different substance. It is observed only when a chemical reaction happens. Examples include flammability (ability to burn), reactivity with acid, reactivity with oxygen (such as rusting) and the ability to decompose when heated. A substance has the chemical property even if it is not reacting at the moment. Noble gases are very unreactive, so they have almost no chemical properties of this kind.
Physical and Chemical Changes: In a physical change the form of a substance changes but its identity stays the same; examples are melting, freezing, boiling, dissolving, cutting and breaking. In a chemical change one or more new substances form with new properties. Signs of a chemical change include a gas (bubbles), a precipitate (a new solid), a color change that is not simply mixing, light or heat given off and a new odor. Atoms are rearranged, not created or destroyed, so the total mass stays the same in a closed system (conservation of mass).
Density: Density is the amount of mass in a unit of volume: density = mass / volume. Common units are g/cm^3 for solids and liquids and kg/m^3 in SI, where 1 g/cm^3 = 1000 kg/m^3. The volume of a regular solid can be found from its dimensions and the volume of an irregular solid by water displacement. A substance has a fixed density at a given temperature, so density helps to identify it. An object floats in a liquid if it is less dense than the liquid and sinks if it is more dense. Water has a density of 1.0 g/cm^3 and ice is less dense than liquid water.
